entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4793"/><div sID="gen6983" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4793"/><hi type="bold">5. strengthen ... with ... mouth--</hi>bitter irony. In allusion to Eliphaz' boasted "consolations" (<reference osisRef="Job.15.11">Job 15:11</reference>). Opposed to strengthening with the heart, that is, with real consolation. Translate, "I also (like you) could strengthen with the mouth," that is, with heartless talk: "And the moving of my lips (mere lip comfort) could console (in the same fashion as you do)" [Umbreit]. "Hearty counsel" (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.9">Pr 27:9</reference>) is the opposite. <div eID="gen6983" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4796"/><div sID="gen6988" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4796"/><hi type="bold">8. filled ... with wrinkles--</hi>Rather (as also the same Hebrew word in <reference osisRef="Job.22.16">Job 22:16</reference>; English Version, "cut down"), "thou hast fettered me, thy witness" (besides cutting off my "band of witnesses," <reference osisRef="Job.16.7">Job 16:7</reference>), that is, hast disabled me by pains from properly attesting my innocence. But another "witness" arises against him, namely, his "leanness" or wretched state of body, construed by his friends into a proof of his guilt. The radical meaning of the Hebrew is "to draw together," whence flow the double meaning "to bind" or "fetter," and in Syriac, "to wrinkle."<div eID="gen6988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6989" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">leanness--</hi>meaning also "lie"; implying it was a "false witness." <div eID="gen6989" type="x-p"/>

But another "witness" arises against him, namely, his "leanness" or wretched state of body, construed by his friends into a proof of his guilt. The radical meaning of the Hebrew is "to draw together," whence flow the double meaning "to bind" or "fetter," and in Syriac, "to wrinkle." leanness-- meaning also "lie"; implying it was a "false witness."

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4804"/><div sID="gen7009" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4804"/><hi type="bold">16. foul--</hi>rather, "is red," that is, flushed and heated [Umbreit and Noyes].<div eID="gen7009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7010" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shadow of death--</hi>that is, darkening through many tears (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.17">La 5:17</reference>). So <reference osisRef="Job.16.10">Job 16:10</reference> above answers to the description of Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.13">Psa 22:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.50.6">Is 50:6</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Job.16.4">Job 16:4</reference> to <reference osisRef="Ps.22.7">Psa 22:7</reference>). He alone realized what Job aspired after, namely, outward righteousness of acts and inward purity of devotion. Jesus Christ as the representative man is typified in some degree in every servant of God in the Old Testament. <div eID="gen7010" type="x-p"/>

entries.reader_content_plain: 20. Hebrew, "are my scorners"; more forcibly, "my mockers-- my friends!" A heart-cutting paradox [Umbreit]. God alone remains to whom he can look for attestation of his innocence; plaintively with tearful eye, he supplicates for this.

"Oh, that He would plead for a man (namely, me) against God." Job quaintly says, "God must support me against God; for He makes me to suffer, and He alone knows me to be innocent" [Umbreit]. So God helped Jacob in wrestling against Himself (compare <reference osisRef="Job.23.6">Job 23:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.32.25">Ge 32:25</reference>). God in Jesus Christ does plead with God for man (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.26">Ro 8:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.27">27</reference>).<div eID="gen7016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7017" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as a man--</hi>literally, "the Son of man." A prefiguring of the advocacy of Jesus Christ--a boon longed for by Job (<reference osisRef="Job.9.33">Job 9:33</reference>), though the spiritual pregnancy of his own words, designed for all ages, was but little understood by him (<reference osisRef="Ps.80.17">Psa 80:17</reference>).<div eID="gen7017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7018" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for his neighbour--</hi>Hebrew, "friend." Job himself (<reference osisRef="Job.42.8">Job 42:8</reference>) pleaded as intercessor for his "friends," though "his scorners" (<reference osisRef="Job.16.20">Job 16:20</reference>); so Jesus Christ the Son of man (<reference osisRef="Luke.23.34">Lu 23:34</reference>); "for friends" (<reference osisRef="John.15.13-John.15.15">Joh 15:13-15</reference>). <div eID="gen7018" type="x-p"/>
